messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

Case Vignette: "Mr. A."

Mr. A. is a 69-year-old widowed financial analyst who presents to therapy at the urging of his daughter. He describes himself as a "numbers man" who has spent forty years managing portfolios and forecasting market trends-work that has always felt predictable and controllable. He is precise, measured, and speaks with a careful economy of words.

The traumatic event occurred fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Mr. A. and his wife of forty-two years, Carol, were returning from a dinner with friends. She was driving, as she always did at night because his night vision had grown poor. They were stopped at a red light when a pickup truck struck them from behind at high speed. The impact was severe, but Mr. A. recalls the moment with eerie clarity: the sudden jolt, the sound of crumpling metal, and then the silence. He turned to Carol. She was unconscious, her head slumped forward. He remembers saying her name, then shouting it. He remembers the paramedics prying him from the passenger seat. He remembers the hospital waiting room, the fluorescent lights humming, and the young doctor's face before she spoke the words that would split his life in two: "We did everything we could."

In the months that followed, Mr. A. returned to work within two weeks. He told himself that routine was the cure. He sat at his desk, ran his spreadsheets, and answered client emails. But the numbers began to blur. He found himself staring at columns of data, unable to recall what he had just read. He started making small errors-a misplaced decimal, a missed deadline-things that had never happened in his career. His supervisor expressed concern. Mr. A. brushed it off, saying he was tired.

At home, he cannot enter the garage. The sight of the car they replaced-a different make, a different color-triggers a visceral reaction: his throat tightens, his palms sweat, and he feels a cold dread spread through his chest. He has taken to parking on the street, even in the rain. He no longer drives at all. He takes the bus to work, leaving an hour early to account for delays. He tells himself it is about traffic, about his eyesight. But he knows, in the quiet moments, that it is about the red light. He cannot sit at a red light without seeing Carol's head slump forward.

Sleep is a battlefield. He lies in the bed they shared, on his side, staring at the ceiling. When he does drift off, the dreams come: the screech of tires, the impact, the silence. He wakes gasping, his heart pounding, convinced for a moment that she is beside him. He has not moved her pillow. He has not washed her side of the sheets. He tells his daughter it is because he hasn't had time.

His daughter visits every Sunday. She brings casseroles, which he eats mechanically, without tasting. She asks about his day. He says, "Fine." She asks if he has spoken to anyone. He says, "I don't need to talk. I need to get on with it." But he cannot get on with it. He has stopped reading the news, because stories about car accidents send him into a spiral. He has stopped going to the grocery store because the parking lot is too loud, too bright, too much. He orders everything online now.

Last month, his daughter found him in the kitchen at 3 a.m., standing at the counter, holding Carol's coffee mug. He was not crying. He was just standing, staring. She asked what he was doing. He said, "I'm trying to remember her voice. I can't remember her voice." That was when she made the appointment.

Mr. A. sits in the therapy chair with his hands folded in his lap. He is polite, cooperative, but his eyes are hollow. He says, "I don't know why I'm here. I'm not the one who was hurt." He says this without irony. He does not see his own wounds. He only sees the empty side of the bed.

output.reasoning: The sentence 'I'm trying to remember her voice. I can't remember her voice.' captures a specific, paradoxical symptom of traumatic grief and directly precipitates the therapy visit, showing the vignette is written from inside this person's unique experience rather than generic description.
output.rationale: This vignette is grounded in realistic clinical experience through precise, idiosyncratic details (e.g., the exact trigger of the red light, the coffee mug incident, and the specific reason for seeking help) that bring the patient's internal world to life.
